title: Stealing and Atonement
author: M.K. Gandhi (adapted from 'My Experiments with Truth')
summary: These extracts from Gandhiji's autobiography tell how, as a boy, he smoked and stole, and how a clean confession to his father cleansed him. It shows that children learn by imitating others, that they can resist negative influences, and that a sincere confession with a promise never to repeat the wrong is the purest repentance.

Gandhiji and a relative became fond of smoking — not because they liked it, but because they imagined some pleasure in blowing out clouds of smoke. They copied his uncle, collecting the stubs of cigarettes he threw away. As stubs were not always available, they stole coins (coppers) from the servant's pocket money to buy Indian cigarettes, and also smoked the porous stalks of a plant.

Unhappy that they could do nothing without their elders' permission, in sheer disgust they decided to commit suicide. They collected dhatura seeds (a poison) from the jungle, went to Kedarjee Mandir in the evening, put ghee in the temple lamp and had darshan. But their courage failed — what if they did not die instantly? They swallowed only two or three seeds and went to Ramji Mandir to compose themselves. Gandhiji realised it is not as easy to commit suicide as to think about it. The episode made them give up smoking stubs and stealing. Later in life he always considered smoking barbarous, dirty and harmful.

At fifteen he committed a more serious theft: his brother owed about twenty-five rupees, so Gandhiji clipped a bit of gold from his brother's solid-gold armlet and the debt was cleared. The guilt became unbearable. He resolved never to steal again and decided to confess to his father — not out of fear of being beaten (his father never beat them) but fear of the pain he would cause him. He wrote out the confession on a slip of paper, asked for adequate punishment, asked his father not to punish himself for the offence, and pledged never to steal again.

Trembling, he handed it to his father, who was ill and lying on a plain wooden plank. His father read it, tears trickled down his cheeks and wet the paper; he closed his eyes in thought and tore up the note. Gandhiji also cried. 'Those tears of love cleansed my heart, and washed my sin away.' Later he understood it was pure Ahimsa (non-violence), which changes everything it touches. His father's sublime forgiveness was unexpected; Gandhiji believed it was due to his clean confession, which made his father feel safe about him and increased his affection.
Admitting our mistakes honestly, asking for punishment and promising not to repeat them is true atonement. Love and forgiveness (Ahimsa) have unlimited power to reform people.

sa2: Why did Gandhiji and his relative decide to commit suicide?
They were upset by their lack of independence — they could not do anything without their elders' permission — so in sheer disgust they decided to commit suicide.
Why did Gandhiji and his relative steal money from the servant's pocket money?
Cigarette stubs were not always available and gave little smoke, so they stole coins from the servant's pocket money to buy Indian cigarettes.
How did the author and his relative become fond of smoking?
They imagined some pleasure in blowing out clouds of smoke and copied his uncle, who smoked, by collecting and smoking the stubs he threw away.
Why was Gandhiji afraid to confess to his father?
Not because he feared a beating — his father never beat them — but because he was afraid of the pain his confession would cause his father.
What did Gandhiji write in his confession?
He confessed his guilt, asked for adequate punishment, requested his father not to punish himself for the offence, and pledged never to steal again.
sa3: How did Gandhiji's father react to his confession? What lesson did Gandhiji learn from it?

His father read the note, tears ran down his cheeks, he closed his eyes in thought and tore it up without a harsh word. Gandhiji learnt that a clean confession with a promise not to repeat the wrong is the purest repentance, and that love and forgiveness (Ahimsa) have unlimited power to change a person.

or: What lesson did Gandhiji learn from the suicide attempt?

When they swallowed a few dhatura seeds their courage failed and they went to Ramji Mandir to calm down. He realised it was not as easy to commit suicide as to think about it, and it is better to bear one's difficulties. The episode made them give up smoking stubs and stealing coppers.
